newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate set to approve budget before deadline.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate set to approve budget before deadline.

text.p: The Senate on Monday debated a budget accord with broad bipartisan support and White House backing that assured its passage before a midnight deadline that would have forced a government shutdown.

"This is as good as it's going to get," said Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota, his hand on a foot-tall (0.4-metre) paper pile that constituted the bill. "I will attempt to dissuade my colleagues from offering any amendments."

Amendments require agreement of the House of Representatives, but few members were in Washington. Most left after the House passed the measure on Saturday in an overwhelming 370-37 vote. The Senate moved to complete work before fiscal 1997 began at midnight.
The compromise bill grants the president an extra $6.5 billion he requested for domestic spending, with $4 billion of that going to education.
After months of negotiations, House Republicans, anxious to return home and campaign in the weeks before the Nov. 5 election, backed away from demands to slash spending.

Daschle called the shift a "remarkable retreat from the Republican positions of two years ago," when the majority party in Congress had demanded deep cuts in education and the environment and a slowing of Medicare growth that Clinton said would ultimately require cuts in benefits.

Republicans, blamed for two partial government shutdowns that resulted from the disagreements, saw their popularity evaporate in public opinion polls. In recent months Republican leaders have pledged to avoid similar rancorous fights.

The change was underscored by President Bill Clinton's praise for the deal, which he said was "good for America because it continues to move us toward a balanced budget while protecting, not violating, our values."
Acknowledging the necessity of compromise, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said, "If we had the White House, (the budget) would be different."

The bill rolls together six spending bills that would be considered separately in an ordinary year. It also incorporates a once-contentious immigration bill and a badly needed measure to strengthen the thrift insurance fund. And it sells broadcast airwaves and expands anti-terrorism measures.

Once the Senate finishes the budget, its leaders want to move on to bills creating new parks and raising money for existing ones and providing money for airport construction. They also want to vote on a bill ending local-level scrutiny of mutual funds and reforming securities laws. But that may take days because of unresolved problems in the bills.

The spending bill provides $244 billion for the military and about $356 billion for other domestic programmes. The administration had wanted the military budget cut by $3.5 billion and had asked for $10 billion in extra domestic spending.

With the extra $6.5 billion, the Senate grants Clinton's request for $4 billion more for Head Start and other education programmes and raises college student Pell grants to the largest amount in history.

The extra spending will be partially paid for with $2.9 billion raised from the sale of cellular communications airwaves and $3.1 billion in higher bank reserves needed to clean up the last of the savings and loan crisis.

The bill provides $1.1 billion to fight terrorism, $650 million for fighting fires in Western states, $400 million to aid in recovery from Hurricane Fran, $123 million for troop redeployment in Saudi Arabia and $8.8 billion for the war on illegal drugs.
It covers military spending, national parks, education, jobs programmes, environmental protection and law enforcement, the White House, foreign aid, health research, and many other activities.
